sections.html:
Manchester sits on the Merrimack River in south-central New Hampshire, about 20 miles from the Massachusetts border and 58 miles from Boston. The city is in Hillsborough County, which shares its county seat role between Manchester and Nashua, and it had 115,644 residents in 2020. Many buyers commute to Boston or Concord. Close to half of occupied homes are rented, so many sales involve tenants or an owner with several properties.

The city's 2010 Master Plan divides it into 25 neighborhoods, and assessments and house styles change a lot from one to the next.

  • West Side: Amoskeag, Rimmon Heights, Notre Dame/McGregorville, and Piscataquog/Granite Square
  • East Side: North End, Janeville/Corey Square, Hallsville, and Bakersville
  • Outer areas: Youngsville and Goffes Falls

A West Side seller and a Goffes Falls seller deal with the same Board of Assessors and Tax Collector, but the buyer pool and the age of the housing can look very different.

The mills defined Manchester for a century after it incorporated as a city in 1846, so the housing stock is older than most. An older house is more likely to need work before it shows well.

  • Older roofs and chimneys take freeze and thaw cycles every year.
  • Heating systems in 1960s houses are often original or near the end of their life.
  • Homes near the Merrimack, the Piscataquog or Cohas Brook deserve a look at the basement and the flood zone status before listing.

Because a cash offer already accounts for those repairs, owners with deferred work often choose to sell as is.

Elm Street and the riverside mill buildings anchor the downtown picture, but most sellers live well away from them. If your house is far from the Amoskeag district, lead with what is special about your own block: the yard, the parking, the school bus stop, the walk to a corner store.

Manchester taxes follow a year that begins April 1 and ends March 31 (RSA 76:2), using the April inventory. The Board of Assessors decides the value, and the Office of the Tax Collector issues the bill.

Assessors reach value three ways: recent sales of comparable properties, replacement cost less depreciation, and, for income property such as apartments, an income approach. Dividing the levy by total assessed value gives the rate, which is the same for every owner. The state Department of Revenue Administration issues it in October or November.

Two bills arrive each year. The early June bill uses half of the previous year's rate. The late November bill uses the new rate and any assessment changes. You have 30 days from the issue date to pay. The 2025 rate is 20.24 per $1,000, up from 19.58 for 2024, and a separate Central Business Service District rate of 0.462730 applies for 2025.

The path from overdue tax to a city deed starts with interest, reaches a lien in about a year, and can end in a deed after two years.

StepWhat happens
InterestLate taxes accrue 8 percent a year (RSA 76:13)
Notice of ArrearageMailed roughly 30 days after each billing goes out (RSA 76:11-b)
Notice of Impending LienSent by certified mail no less than 30 days ahead of the lien (RSA 80:60)
Lien executedRate jumps to 14 percent a year (RSA 80:69), and the lien is recorded at the Registry of Deeds within 30 days
Mortgagee noticeGoes out 60 days after the lien, with a $10 fee plus any title search cost (RSA 80:67)
Tax deedPossible once two years pass after the lien, following a notice of impending deed at least 30 days before (RSA 80:76, 80:77)

A former owner or mortgagee who wants the property back after a deed must tell the city by certified mail within 30 days of the notice of intent to repurchase, and must prove they can cover back taxes, interest, costs and a 10 percent penalty on the equalized assessed value (RSA 80:89).

Write to the Board of Assessors with an abatement application, and make sure it is received or postmarked by March 1 following the final tax bill. Filing online is not allowed because an original signature is required, and the city charges no fee.

To qualify, you must have owned the property on April 1 of the tax year, or be otherwise aggrieved, and you must demonstrate that it was assessed out of proportion to other property in town. The Board decides by July 1. Silence by then counts as a denial.

  • Any further appeal must be filed by September 1.
  • Pick one route: the State Board of Tax and Land Appeals (written, with a fee) or Hillsborough County Superior Court, Northern District, 300 Chestnut Street, Manchester.
  • Choosing the Board of Tax and Land Appeals means you cannot also petition the Superior Court (RSA 76-B:11).

If an abatement application is still pending when you sell, mention it to the title company, because the decision changes the tax bill for your year of ownership.

Give the title company a heads-up at the very start. At closing, whatever tax is unpaid and any recorded lien are paid from your proceeds. The Tax Collector will provide a copy of a lien release for $10 per property plus $2 per receipt requested, by email at Taxcollector@manchesternh.gov or in person at One City Hall Plaza.

A redeemed lien is released within 30 days, and the release is mailed to the Hillsborough County Register of Deeds, 19 Temple Street, Nashua. Deeds can take 30 days or longer to reach the Assessors, which means a bill may still carry your name after closing. Send the new owner's name and address along in writing.

Under the state's transfer tax, each side pays $0.75 per $100 of price, with a $20 minimum apiece for prices up to $4,000. The stamps are purchased at the register of deeds. Two declarations, CD-57-P for the purchaser and CD-57-S for the seller, plus the PA-34 inventory, are due to the state within 30 days of the deed being recorded.

sections.h2: What buyers will ask about a Manchester house
sections.html:
Neighborhood matters here. A buyer looking at the West Side, the East Side or Goffes Falls will have different expectations for age and condition. Know the age of the roof and heating system, any history of a wet basement, and whether the house sits near the river or the brook. A seller who answers those questions before they are asked usually keeps the deal on track.

The interstates, the Everett Turnpike and the regional airport put many Manchester houses within easy reach of Boston, so mention the nearest on-ramp. A West Side buyer, an East Side buyer and a Goffes Falls buyer each weigh different things, and the best listing language speaks to the actual street, not the city as a whole.

With about half of occupied homes rented, many Manchester sellers are landlords. With tenants in place, pull together the leases, deposit records and rent roll before you speak with a buyer. Find out whether the building is near the river, the Piscataquog or Cohas Brook, since flood status is a common question. A cash buyer can take over a tenant-occupied building as is, but the lease terms still decide how quickly the buyer can use the property.

Landlords should also tell the title company whether the property sits in the Central Business Service District, since that district carries its own added rate.

faqs.q: When is Manchester property tax due?
faqs.a: Each bill is due 30 days after issue. One is mailed in early June and the other in late November, for a tax year that runs April 1 to March 31.

faqs.q: What is the interest rate on late Manchester property tax?
faqs.a: 8 percent per year on unpaid taxes under RSA 76:13. Once a tax lien is executed, interest on the lien is 14 percent per year under RSA 80:69.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Manchester house if there is a tax lien on it?
faqs.a: Yes. The lien is paid from the sale proceeds and released after payment, and a full redemption leads to a release within 30 days. Ask the Tax Collector for the current payoff before closing.

faqs.q: Who pays the New Hampshire transfer tax when a house sells?
faqs.a: Both. The buyer and the seller each pay $0.75 per $100 of the price, though transfers by will or intestate succession are exempt.

faqs.q: Where do I appeal a Manchester assessment after the Board of Assessors denies it?
faqs.a: File by September 1 with either the State Board of Tax and Land Appeals or Hillsborough County Superior Court, Northern District. You pick one, and choosing the state board waives the court option.
